📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

In a recent development, while Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

In a recent development, for a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

It has been revealed that while traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a significant plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

Provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

Forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

Unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

According to recent reports, use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

According to recent reports, for a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

Sources indicate that bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

According to recent reports, once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

Sources indicate that cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a newly introduced element to traditional holiday greenery too.

A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

Position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

Scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

It has been revealed that at this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

For a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

It's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

A few simple practices will keep your aromatic holiday houseplants fresh and fragrant:.

Puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

Sources indicate that the opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Sources indicate that puppies learn quickly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

Recent findings suggest that all puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Industry observers note that food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health challenges is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

In a recent development, puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Sources indicate that most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health concerns. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

In a recent development, some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the new plants a little boost.

Sources indicate that nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

Nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

In a recent development, moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

In a recent development, sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

According to recent reports, the most crucial part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

According to recent reports, hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Recent findings suggest that hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

It has been revealed that calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

It has been revealed that like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

While cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

While all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

Remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

According to recent reports, if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

It has been revealed that chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, Newly introduced York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Sources indicate that chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

In a recent development, chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, swiftly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

Sources indicate that in 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

Industry observers note that in January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

It has been revealed that chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Industry observers note that support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

According to recent reports, keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

In a recent development, follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

According to recent reports, among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!
  • Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval!
  • In a recent development, this underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

In a recent development, this underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

Recent findings suggest that for me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, indicates, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

It has been revealed that remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

Industry observers note that for a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

Fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks indicates fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

It has been revealed that drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

According to recent reports, dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.
  • Whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard. These mysterious nighttime visitors can be surprisingly elusive, but there are ways to make your garden a more welcoming place for them. And no, you don't need acres of woodland or a sprawling country estate to get your very own owl hangout started.

The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.

Whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey. And the good news? Well, you can make a surprisingly big difference with just five plants.

It has been revealed that that's right, folks! If you want more owls in your garden, that means providing shelter for small mammals, encouraging insects and other prey, and offering trees and shrubs where owls can perch, roost or potentially nest.

From tall native grasses to berry-producing shrubs and evergreen trees, then, these are some of the best additions for creating an owl-friendly backyard.

Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a fantastic native grass for an owl-friendly garden, particularly if you have a sunny spot where you can let it grow relatively undisturbed.

Sources indicate that why? Well, because its tall stems and dense clumps provide valuable cover for small mammals, including voles and mice, which are important prey for many owl species. The grass also offers shelter for other wildlife through winter, when more exposed parts of the garden can become less hospitable.

Switchgrass is particularly useful in meadow-style plantings, where it can grow alongside native wildflowers. It produces attractive seedheads in late summer and fall, too, and it's a relatively low-maintenance perennial once established.

Give it a sunny position and well-drained soil, then, and leave some of its growth standing over winter rather than cutting everything back in fall. You may just find it swiftly becomes your latest favorite garden plant, let alone the best part of your owl hangout!

Sources indicate that if you want to make your garden more appealing to owls, don't underestimate the value of evergreen trees! Native pines and spruces provide year-round cover, with dense branches offering potential daytime roosting spots and sheltered perches. Their evergreen foliage can also make wildlife feel more protected from disturbance and exposure.

Sources indicate that different owl species have different preferences, but trees are an crucial part of the habitat for many woodland-dwellers like barred owls. Some species also use natural cavities in mature trees for nesting.

According to recent reports, if you have room, consider something like this stunning Eastern White Pine from Nature Hills. Just remember that a newly planted sapling is unlikely to become an instant owl retreat, though, so it's always better to preserve mature trees where you can!

Sources indicate that A slightly wild patch of blackberry brambles (Rubus spp.) might not be everyone's idea of a perfectly manicured garden, but it's a genius addition to anyone hoping to turn their yard into an owl hangout. After all, blackberry thickets provide dense cover for small critters and nesting birds, not to mention food and shelter for plenty others besides.

Why does this matter for owls? Because a garden that supports a healthy range of small animals can help provide the prey that visiting owls need, of course! And you don't have to let blackberries take over your entire yard, either. A small patch of something like Baby Cakes® Blackberry Bush from Nature Hills along a boundary or at the back of a wildlife-friendly border can provide plenty of habitat value.

Just remember that brambles can spread, so give them room and keep growth away from paths and areas where people regularly walk.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) is a beautiful native shrub or small tree that brings several seasons of wildlife interest to the garden; think white flowers that attract pollinators, followed by edible berries in summer, which are enjoyed by birds and other wildlife.

Its value doesn't stop with the berries; serviceberry also supports insects and provides useful woody cover, helping to create a more diverse backyard habitat. For an owl-friendly garden, this is all about supporting the wider food web... but hey, it helps that it's a stunner, too!

Industry observers note that goldenrod (Solidago spp.) is often overlooked as a wildlife plant, but its bright yellow flowers provide an key late-season source of nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies and other insects. Those insects, in turn, help support other wildlife, including small birds and mammals.

It has been revealed that some smaller owl species also eat large insects, making insect-rich habitats like goldenrod a must for your owl hangout! Especially as it's a lovely way to add late-summer and fall color to your garden. Many varieties are native to North America, and once established, they're generally easy to grow.

Something like the Fireworks Solidago (Goldenrod) Plant from Burpee is a great way to go!

Industry observers note that these five plants are a great starting point for your owl hangout, but there are plenty of other native choices that can help make your backyard more wildlife-friendly. #.

In a recent development, viburnums, for example, produce berries that feed birds and other wildlife, while their dense branching offers useful cover, too. Native dogwoods offer flowers, berries and dense branching that can provide shelter for wildlife, not to mention some much-added beauty to any yard (there's a reason they're swiftly replacing magnolias for a lot of people!).

Junipers offer dense year-round cover and provide berry-like cones that are eaten by birds and small mammals. And purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea) attract pollinators and produce seedheads that feed birds and other critters, too.

Sources indicate that of course, planting is a brilliant starting point, but there are a few other things you can do to make your garden more appealing to these fascinating birds. As ever, try leaving some areas of longer grass and natural vegetation rather than tidying every corner. Keep mature trees where possible, particularly those with natural cavities, and consider whether a species-appropriate owl nest box might be suitable for your local area.

It has been revealed that it's also notable to avoid rodent poisons, as owls can be exposed to rodenticides when they eat poisoned mice and rats. Keep lights to a minimum after the sun goes down, as they can confuse nocturnal birds and critters. And, finally, remember that owls need peace and quiet; take care to avoid disturbing potential roosting and nesting areas, particularly during breeding season.

Sources indicate that you might not spot an owl straight away, but by planting for wildlife and allowing your garden to become a little more natural, you'll be creating a much richer habitat for all sorts of visitors. And who knows? Before too long, your owl hangout might just be the most buzzing nightspot in town...

Bringing Your Citrus Trees Indoors for Winter? Get These 6 Things Right to Avoid Leaf Drop and Pests

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun.
  • Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after.
  • Industry observers note that that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun. Then the cold arrives. Citrus can't take a hard freeze, so in colder climates, potted trees have to come inside for winter.

The move itself is a shock, though. Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after. Indoor light is weaker, the air is drier, and pests that rode in on the branches can spread to nearby houseplants.

Industry observers note that that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike. Six checks before the tree comes through the door can head off much of that.

Recent findings suggest that most citrus can be damaged below 32°F (0°C), and a potted tree is more exposed than one in the ground. Lemons and limes are usually the most tender, while kumquats, satsumas, and calamondins can handle a little more chill. Aim to have the tree inside before nights start dipping into the 40s (4–9°C). Wait for the first freeze warning, and you'll be dragging a heavy pot from full sun straight indoors. Give it a week or two in a shady spot near the house first instead – it adjusts to lower light that way.

Flip the leaves over and look along the midvein. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) shows up there as small, flat, tan bumps. Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) leave pale speckles and, eventually, fine webbing where the leaf meets the stem, and white, cottony clumps in the leaf joints usually mean citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri).

If you find anything, spray the tree outdoors with an insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil labeled for citrus, such as Monterey horticultural oil concentrate. Blueprint on more than one round. Once inside, keep it away from other houseplants for three or four weeks.

Industry observers note that bugs don't only ride in on the leaves. Tip the pot on its side, look in the drainage holes, and lift the saucer. Slugs, sowbugs, and earwigs all like that damp spot underneath, and ants sometimes leave small piles of potting mix they've hauled out. A slow soak with the hose drives many of them out.

Check any roots poking through the holes, too. Firm, light-colored roots are a good sign, but dark, mushy ones and a sour smell point to waterlogged soil. Unless the roots are in real trouble, wait to repot citrus trees until spring.

Citrus needs far more light than a pothos or snake plant. Indoors, aim for at least six hours of bright light a day. A south- or southwest-facing window is usually the best spot, with the tree close to the glass but not touching it. Up north, short winter days often fall short – that's when a grow light helps. Glowrium sells a dual-head LED grow light on Amazon that's just under 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, with heads that bend toward the canopy. Trees moved from full sun to a dim corner overnight often shed a good share of their leaves.

Hold a hand over a heating vent or radiator when the heat kicks on. That hot, dry air blows straight across the leaves of a nearby tree, and a cold, drafty window or door is no better. Sudden swings like those commonly trigger leaf drop. Somewhere around 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night, about 55–65°F (13–18°C), works well.

Humidity near 50% helps in a heated house. The Pure Enrichment MistAire humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours on a tank, and the ThermoPro digital hygrometer can sit by the pot to track both.

In a recent development, on a hot patio, potted citrus can need water every day or two. Indoors, with cooler rooms and less light, it uses much less, and the summer routine can drown the roots. Push a finger about 2 inches (5 cm) into the mix, and water only when it feels dry at that depth. Deep pots are harder to judge, which is where a moisture meter, like the Xlux Long Probe Plant Soil Moisture Meter, is invaluable.

Water until some drains out, then empty the saucer. Set the pot on a few terra-cotta Pot Toes to keep the drainage holes clear. Don't overcorrect, though – a tree left bone dry for long stretches drops flowers and can lose leaves.

Some leaf drop in the first few weeks is common. Less light, drier air, and new temperatures all hit at once, and a few leaves on the floor are just part of it, mostly.

In a recent development, look closer if leaves keep falling after the first month or whole branches go bare. A wet, sour-smelling mix points to overwatering, while a mix that's dry all the way down means it went too long between drinks. Check how close the tree sits to a vent or cold door, and whether that window is as bright in December as it seemed in October. Sticky spots, webbing, or cottony clumps under the leaves mean pests got past the quarantine.

Get through those six checks, and your tree has an easier winter ahead. Come spring, once nights stay above 50°F (10°C), it can head back out to the patio a little at a time.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Latest Update: This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective.
  • Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones.
  • Sources indicate that we all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective. It’s so disappointing when a Schlumbergera isn’t showing even the smallest pinpricks of colored buds on its stem ends by late fall, especially if you’ve been diligently delivering all the care your Christmas cactus needs in November. But by shifting your stubborn plant into survival mode, you can kickstart its bloom cycle. And guess what? All you need is a banana and a plastic bag.

Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones. This causes the plants to stop growing green leaf segments and switch to developing flowerbuds. And you can use the exact same idea with the natural chemicals a ripe banana releases if your Christmas cactus isn't blooming yet.

Sources indicate that we all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast. That’s down to the ethylene it emits, a natural hormone that plants release when nearing the end of their life cycle. So, by trapping ethylene around your Christmas cactus for a short time, you can trick the plant into thinking it’s under extreme threat, which triggers it to develop flowers as a last-ditch survival effort to preserve its genetics via seed production. Clever, huh?

Highly ripe bananas that have brown spots or are turning brown emit the highest levels of ethylene. You only need to use the peel: though the whole fruit produces ethylene gas, the soft, sweet flesh of a banana is a magnet for fruit flies and fungus gnats and adds too much moisture to the little greenhouse you’re about to create.

Excess moisture will quickly evaporate from the inner surface of the peel, further reducing humidity and any risk of pests or disease.

Now stand your Christmas cactus, still in its container, on a plate or significant plant saucer and lay the banana peel alongside the pot base. It’s important that the peel doesn’t touch the leaf segments or soil as this risks transferring mold or fungal spores.

Sources indicate that pull a clear plastic bag down over the plant, plate and banana peel, and tuck or tie under the plate to seal. If the bag is flimsy and falls onto the stems, use chopsticks or skewers poked into the soil to create a frame so there's no direction contact between plant and plastic.

It has been revealed that it’s vital the bag is clear as an opaque bag is likely to take the stress a step too far and your plant may drop leaf segments instead of developing buds. It also means you can keep a close eye on your plant through the process. A clear unscented trash bag like this from Amazon is ideal as it's plenty big enough to make fashioning your mini-greenhouse easy.

Now your Christmas cactus is in its little greenhouse, it’ll swiftly overheat if it’s hit by the sun’s rays so find it a spot in a bright room but out of direct sunlight.

According to recent reports, the optimum amount of time to leave your Schlumbergera in its ethylene tank is exactly 2 days and 2 nights. This gives the gas plenty of time to chemically shock the plant and trigger bud development, without damaging the plant or giving mold a chance to develop in the restricted air circulation.

Sources indicate that while professional growers use incredibly precise parts-per-million doses of synthetic chemicals, you can’t tell exactly how much ethylene your chosen banana is emitting. So, keep an eye on your Christmas cactus and if at any point the plant looks like it’s struggling or there’s the slightest sign of mold, remove the bag straight away. Don’t be tempted to leave the bag on any longer than 48 hours as too much ethylene can harm bud development.

Carefully take off the plastic bag, discard the peel and place your plant in the spot where you want it to flower, being sure to avoid these Christmas cactus disaster zones. After a week or so, you should see pinhead-sized bumps starting to form on the leaf segment tips and by two weeks, they should be clearly visible.

It’s vital you check your plant hasn’t already begun developing buds before trying this trick. Inspect leaf tips under a bright light – or use a cheap magnifying glass with LED light like this from Amazon – to look for any bumps beginning to form right on the tips of the leaf segments. These may be tiny so gently feel for them with a fingertip, too. If your Schlumbergera has pink or red flowers these little bumps will be bright but if your plant blooms white they may be green and harder to spot.

If you’re in any doubt, wait a week and see if those bumps get any bigger. While using ethylene from ripe banana peel is a very effective way to get a Christmas cactus to flower, this hormone shock can also cause existing buds to stall if the process has already begun.

If this pro growers' trick doesn’t work, there’s likely an underlying reason why your Christmas cactus isn't flowering, that’s overriding the plant’s system.

It has been revealed that the banana bag trick is well worth trying if your Christmas cactus doesn’t have buds yet, and you still just have enough time to trigger your plant into producing flowers for the holidays. Next year, be sure to use the black-out hack that tricks your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time, and you won’t have to worry!

Meet The Christmas Tree That Flowers In Summer – This Stunning Evergreen Puts On A Spectacular Display

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you think of a Christmas tree, chances are you picture a familiar fir or spruce, perhaps decorated with twinkling lights and festive ornaments. But, for some people, Christmas looks a little different.

That's right; instead of bringing an evergreen indoors, many people celebrate the season beneath a spectacular flowering tree covered in brilliant red blooms. Meet the Latest Zealand Christmas Tree, also known as the pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). This extraordinary evergreen puts on one of the most eye-catching floral displays of summer, transforming coastlines and gardens with masses of vibrant crimson flowers.

And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...

Shop Flowering Christmas Trees:.

It has been revealed that native to New Zealand, the pōhutukawa has earned its festive nickname thanks to its spectacular flowering season, which coincides with Christmas in the Southern Hemisphere. Because, while much of the northern hemisphere is welcoming winter with bare branches and chilly temperatures, New Zealand is enjoying the height of summer... and that's when this remarkable tree really comes into its own.

Industry observers note that rather than having conventional petals, its unmistakable flowers look just like fluffy red brushes (which pollinators love). And, against the tree's glossy green leaves, the effect is nothing short of spectacular.

A post shared by Hahana (@hahana_official).

Although it can reach around 65 feet tall in its natural habitat, younger New Zealand Christmas trees can be grown from seed in large containers (although they need plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil and protection from frost).

For US gardeners, growing one outdoors will generally be limited to warmer and frost-free USDA Zones, so it isn't necessarily a practical choice for everyone. Luckily, though, there are other flowering evergreens that can deliver a similarly spectacular effect...

If it's the striking crimson display of the pōhutukawa that catches your eye, bottlebrush is perhaps the closest alternative when it comes to finding a flowering evergreen that might serve well as a Christmas tree. Especially as its bright red blooms have plenty in common with the Kiwi native.

Depending on the variety and climate, bottlebrush (available at Walmart) can flower from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. Many varieties are evergreen and container-friendly, too, although they prefer a sunny position and well-drained soil.

For gardeners who love the idea of a flowering Christmas tree, but prefer something with more traditional-looking blooms, southern magnolia is a beautiful option, as its enormous (and fabulously fragranced) flowers can measure up to 12 inches across.

Industry observers note that while it doesn't have the bright red flowers of the pōhutukawa, it shares some of its most appealing qualities: year-round evergreen foliage, a substantial tree-like presence and an impressive summer floral display. For smaller spaces, consider a compact cultivar such as this 'Little Gem' from Expert Gardener. It has a naturally narrower growth habit than many full-sized southern magnolias, making it a more manageable choice for smaller gardens.

It can also be grown in a large container so long as you treat it to sufficient room, good drainage and consistent moisture.

If fragrance is just as important as appearance, gardenia is another gorgeous Christmas tree alternative thanks to its deep-green foliage and exquisite white flowers.

According to recent reports, oh sure, their blooms may be smaller than those of the southern magnolia, but they more than make up for it with their intoxicating perfume. And, as they don't naturally grow into large trees, standard-trained gardenias can make particularly attractive container garden options; generally best suited to warmer USDA growing zones, growing them in pots makes it easier to protect them from cold weather.

Something like the Frost Proof Gardenia from Nature Hills is happily able to handle temperatures down to 0-10°F, too!

The Fresh Zealand Christmas Tree is a wonderful reminder that evergreens don't have to be all about foliage; indeed, some of the most spectacular trees and shrubs combine year-round greenery with extraordinary seasonal flowers.

Whether you choose the fiery red blooms of bottlebrush, the impressive flowers of southern magnolia or the beautiful fragrance of gardenia, there's no shortage of ways to bring that flowering-evergreen look into your own garden. And who knows? You might even find yourself looking at your Christmas tree traditions a little differently as a result...

How to Spot a Houseplant With Spider Mites – and Prayer Plants are #1 Victims This Month

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves.
  • According to recent reports, as soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive.
  • In a recent development, spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves. While spider mites can target any houseplant, prayer plants are the most commonly affected, with monstera and alocasia close behind. So, if you're disappointed to discover some houseplant leaves fading, looking dusty or appearing speckled with tiny spots at this time of year, don’t presume it's just dust: check to see if your houseplant has spider mites straight away.

According to recent reports, as soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive. The time it takes for these pests to reproduce reduces as temperatures rise, and in cozy conditions a single spider mite can turn into a thousand in a couple of weeks. Which is why, when mid-November arrives, numbers suddenly explode and we start spotting spider-mite infestations in houseplants.

In a recent development, spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too. These common houseplant pests can be easily managed, though, and the earlier you catch the problem, the easier it is to deal with. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a spider mite infestation.

Sources indicate that first, rule out dust by wiping the houseplant's leaves with a soft, damp cloth. Then look for these signs that signal you could be dealing with a spider mite infestation:.

Spider mites are actually arachnids, like spiders, not mites. They are extremely small – about a half a millimeter – and generally gather on the undersides of leaves. Here they pierce the leaves and suck out the contents to feed. The resulting damage from these feeding spots are very small, pale dots on the tops of foliage that can’t be wiped away, and these speckled leaves are a tell-tale sign of an infestation. As the population of spider mites grows, you’ll start to see fine silk webbing, which can easily be mistaken for dusty houseplant leaves.

Houseplants with broad, thin leaves that are easy to pierce are the most favored. While prayer plants are the most commonly attacked, monstera, alocasia, ficus, croton, palms, English ivy and dracaena are also highly susceptible to these pests.

It has been revealed that early intervention is the key to success if you have a houseplant with a spider mite infestation. But, even if you're dealing with a heavy infestation, these steps will work, though you'll need to repeat them to break the spider mite lifecycle.

It's vital to keep the affected plant away from other houseplants as spider mites can easily move from one plant to another. Move it to a different, plant-free room until the problem has been resolved. Now that you know what to look for, check all your other houseplants very carefully for early, subtle signs of an infestation.

Next, you want to get rid of as many of the mites as you can. The easiest way to do this is to place your houseplant in the shower or bathtub and give it a good rinse. Use a firm stream of water so the pressure rinses most of the pests off, but ensure the jet isn't so harsh that it damages the plant.

Sources indicate that be sure to direct the water to the undersides of leaves where the mites are feeding and at any webbing you can see. Follow the rinse with a thorough wiping with a damp cloth to remove any webbing still attached. This process is unlikely to remove all the mites or their eggs, so repeat the process every few days as fresh eggs hatch.

In a recent development, regular rinsing reduces a spider mite population but it doesn't remove it entirely. To fully break the lifecycle, you'll need an insecticidal soap with a natural formula such as NatureStop Insecticidal Soap, available from Amazon, or a neem oil spray like Captain Jack's Need Oil Spray for Plants, also on Amazon. These organic options will treat indoor plant pests safely. Insecticidal soap kills mites on contact by breaking down their cell membranes, while neem oil disrupts feeding and reproduction and smothers pests.

In a recent development, follow the label instructions for whichever product you choose and be sure to cover all areas of the plant, including undersides of leaves and stems. This is key as both products work by direct contact with the mites. Repeat the application as often as suggested on the label, as you’ll likely need several applications to get rid of pests completely.

Remove any badly damaged leaves, whether they're heavily stippled, have turned mostly yellow or have brown, crispy areas. Snip off with sharp pruners and dispose of them in the garbage (not the compost). Any foliage that's mostly green can be left and, while damaged leaves won’t return to their former glory, healthy areas will still photosynthesize and support the plant’s recovery.

Good houseplant care in fall will make conditions less favorable to spider mites:.

If houseplant leaves have irregular patches of white or light gray powder on their surfaces that can be wiped away, this is likely a fungal infection, powdery mildew and should be treated by disposing of heavily affected leaves and using a product like neem oil or a commercial houseplant fungicide. A white film or larger spots could be mineral deposits from watering If you have hard water and mist or irrigate houseplants from above, easily fixed by cleaning leaves then avoiding getting foliage wet.

A lost leaf or two doesn’t spell disaster for a Christmas cactus in fall but you can't afford to ignore this distress signal.

#55994. Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1181 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass.
  • Fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder.
  • Industry observers note that this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

Fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

Industry observers note that this year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

In a recent development, many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

According to recent reports, it’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

Sources indicate that instead of endlessly raking, run a mulching mower, like this Greenworks model, over the grass as needed, chopping up the leaves when you see light to moderate coverage. Another option is to remove some of a thick layer of leaves for use in compost or as a mulch in beds. Don’t worry about removing every last leaf before winter.

According to recent reports, fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

Sources indicate that A simple rain gauge, such as this easy-to-read JMBay model from Amazon, can help you keep track of rainfall. Keep an eye on the soil and rain and decide when the grass could use a deep drink rather than sticking with a strict schedule.

In a recent development, of course, there are exceptions. If you have seeded parts of the lawn or installed upcoming sod before winter, these areas should be watered regularly right up until the ground freezes.

At some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but initiative to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

Keep mowing to the recommended height for your type of grass until the final cut. A tool like the Oregon Deck Leveling Gauge from Amazon can help you check your mower's cutting height and ensure an even cut.

It has been revealed that as growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

Bagging all of your healthy grass clippings is unnecessary. It’s also a highly labor-intensive chore. Don’t waste your time, energy, or back on this one. Finely chopped grass decomposes promptly and adds nutrients to the soil. And, contrary to popular belief, grass clippings left on the ground do not contribute to thatch buildup.

In a recent development, instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer big clumps you'll get.

Sources indicate that managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

Instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

Fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

Industry observers note that cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

Your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

Instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

Industry observers note that as you proposal fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.

💡 Key Takeaways
